questions.stem: A client taking furosemide has a potassium level of 3.1 mEq/L. Which finding on the rhythm strip should the nurse expect?

options.text: Flat T waves with a U wave after the T
No change from a normal beat

questions.explanation: B is correct: a potassium of 3.1 is below the normal 3.5, and low potassium flattens the T wave and makes the U wave visible. A and C are signs of high potassium, not low. D is wrong because low potassium does change the strip.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews a normal beat on the rhythm strip. Which wave represents the ventricles resetting?
questions.explanation: C is correct: the T wave is the ventricles resetting. A, the P wave, is the atria firing and contracting. B, the tall spike, is the ventricles firing and contracting. D, the U wave, is a tiny bump after the T, normally barely seen.

questions.stem: An order reads: potassium chloride 20 mEq, push into a vein. What is the nurse's best action?

options.text: Give it as a shot into the muscle instead
Hold the dose and clarify the order with the provider
Give half now and half in an hour

questions.explanation: C is correct: potassium is never pushed into a vein, so the nurse holds it and clarifies with the provider. A is still a push. B is wrong because potassium is never given as a shot into the muscle. D is still a push and changes the order without the provider.

questions.stem: The nurse is preparing intravenous potassium through a peripheral line. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run it on an infusion pump
Confirm urine output is at least 30 mL per hour
Infuse about 40 mEq in one hour
Push it slowly if the pump is unavailable

questions.explanation: A, B, C, and D are correct: potassium is a high-alert medication, so it is diluted, run on a pump, and double-checked, and urine output of at least 30 mL an hour shows the kidneys can clear it. E is wrong because peripheral infusion is about 10 mEq an hour max, per policy. F is wrong because potassium is never pushed.

questions.stem: Before hanging an intravenous potassium infusion, the nurse notes urine output of 15 mL per hour for the last 2 hours. What is the priority action?

options.text: Hold the infusion and notify the provider
Increase the infusion rate to finish sooner
Give the potassium by mouth instead

questions.explanation: B is correct: urine output should be at least 30 mL an hour before giving potassium because the kidneys have to clear it, and 15 mL an hour is too low. A risks potassium building up. C is unsafe: faster infusion raises the danger. D changes the route without an order and does not fix the kidney concern.

questions.stem: Which client is at highest risk for a high potassium level?

options.text: A client with vomiting and diarrhea
A client taking a thiazide diuretic

questions.explanation: C is correct: kidney failure is the number one cause of high potassium because the kidneys can't get rid of it. A and D are loop and thiazide diuretics, which waste potassium and cause low potassium. B loses potassium, causing low potassium.

questions.stem: Which medications can raise a client's potassium level? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A, B, and E are correct: spironolactone spares potassium so it builds up, Ace inhibitors raise it, and potassium chloride adds it. C and D are loop and thiazide diuretics that make the kidneys waste potassium.

questions.stem: A client with a potassium of 6.8 mEq/L has peaked T waves on the monitor. Which medication is the priority?
questions.explanation: B is correct: rhythm changes at a potassium of 6.8 mean the heart is in danger, and intravenous calcium gluconate protects the heart first. A and C remove potassium, but that comes later and works more slowly. D would raise potassium further.

questions.stem: The nurse gives intravenous calcium gluconate to a client with high potassium. Which statement about this drug is accurate?

options.text: It lowers the potassium level quickly
It protects the heart but does not lower potassium
It shifts potassium into the cells
It removes potassium through the kidneys

questions.explanation: B is correct: calcium gluconate protects the heart but does not lower potassium. A is wrong for the same reason. C describes regular insulin plus dextrose. D describes diuretics.

questions.stem: After intravenous regular insulin plus dextrose is given for high potassium, which assessment is most important to follow up?
questions.explanation: A is correct: insulin plus dextrose shifts potassium into the cells, and insulin can cause low blood sugar, so check glucose next. B, reflexes, is the check for magnesium. C, urine color, and D, pupil size, don't detect the main risk of this treatment.
